e-8256.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable
e-8256.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} 
= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =[-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot 1+[-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})]\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t})-t{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}) \\  & =-(1+t){e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t{e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

e-8257.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
e-8257.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\sqrt{x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-8258.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
e-8258.problem: Let $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2,$ where $x = s\cos{t}$ and $y = t\sin{s}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
e-8258.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y = y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2t\operatorname{sin}⁡s)(\operatorname{sin}⁡s) \\  & =-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t{sin}^{2}⁡s \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-2{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2t{sin}^{2}⁡s-{s}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the identity $\sin 2t = 2\sin t\cos t$ in the above simplification.

e-8259.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables
e-8259.problem: Let $f(x,y,z) = e^{xy + z},$ where $x = s + t,$ $y = s-t$ and $z = -s^2.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$
e-8259.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t), y = y(s,t)$ and $z = z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\cdot \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x, y$ and $z\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{xy+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(s-t){e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}=(s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(s+t){e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}=(s+t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s+t)(s-t)-{s}^{2}}={e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot 1+(s+t){e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot (-1)+{e}^{-{t}^{2}}\cdot 0 \\  & =(s-t-s-t){e}^{-{t}^{2}} \\  & =-2t{e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{2xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot 1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=2xy,x=t and y=ln⁡t, compute dfdt.

a
12ln⁡t
b
2+ttln⁡t
c
ln⁡t2tln⁡t
d
1+ln⁡t2tln⁡t
e
1+t2ln⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows: dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=y2xy,∂f∂y=x2xy

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get ∂f∂x=ln⁡t2tln⁡t,∂f∂y=t2tln⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=1,dydt=1t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=ln⁡t2tln⁡t⋅1+t2tln⁡t⋅1t=ln⁡t2tln⁡t+12tln⁡t=1+ln⁡t2tln⁡t.

verification.explanation: The chain rule gives df/dt = ln(t)/√(2t ln(t)) + [t/√(2t ln(t))](1/t) = (1+ln(t))/√(2t ln(t)). This confirms option d and agrees with the revealed solution; option c omits the contribution from y.

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{2xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot 1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(xy2),x=cos⁡t and y=sin⁡t, compute dfdt for 0<t<π2.

a
2tan⁡t−cot⁡t
b
sec⁡t−tan⁡t
c
2csc⁡t−tan⁡t
d
2cot⁡t−tan⁡t
e
cot⁡t+2csc⁡t
Submit

decision.explanation: On the given interval, f(t)=ln(cos(t))+2ln(sin(t)). Differentiating gives df/dt=−tan(t)+2cot(t), which matches option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}=\frac{2}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{cot}⁡t-\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(xy2),x=cos⁡t and y=sin⁡t, compute dfdt for 0<t<π2.

a
2tan⁡t−cot⁡t
b
sec⁡t−tan⁡t
c
2csc⁡t−tan⁡t
d
2cot⁡t−tan⁡t
e
cot⁡t+2csc⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=y2xy2=1x,∂f∂y=2xyxy2=2y

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=1cos⁡t,∂f∂y=2sin⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=−sin⁡t,dydt=cos⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=1cos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+2sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t=−sin⁡tcos⁡t+2⋅cos⁡tsin⁡t=2cot⁡t−tan⁡t.

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{cot}⁡t-\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}=\frac{2}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{cot}⁡t-\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

If f(x,y)=x2ey,x=2t and y=t2, compute dfdt.

a
4t(1+2t)et2
b
8t3(2+t)et2
c
8t(1+t2)et2
d
 2t2(1+t2)et2
e
4t(2+t)et2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xey,∂f∂y=x2ey

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=2(2t)et2=4tet2,∂f∂y=(2t)2et2=4t2et2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=2,dydt=2t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=4tet2⋅2+4t2et2⋅2t=8tet2+8t3et2=8t(1+t2)et2.

verification.explanation: The chain rule gives df/dt=(4te^(t²))(2)+(4t²e^(t²))(2t)=8t(1+t²)e^(t²). This matches option c and confirms the revealed worked solution.

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$

Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=xy,x=cos⁡2s and y=sin⁡2s, compute dfds.

a
cot⁡2s
b
tan⁡2s+csc2⁡2s
c
2sec2⁡2s
d
tan⁡2s
e
−2csc2⁡2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows: dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=1y,∂f∂y=−xy2

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get ∂f∂x=1sin⁡2s,∂f∂y=−cos⁡2ssin2⁡2s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get dxds=−2sin⁡2s,dyds=2cos⁡2s.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=1sin⁡2s⋅(−2sin⁡2s)+(−cos⁡2ssin2⁡2s)⋅2cos⁡2s=−2−2⋅cos2⁡2ssin2⁡2s=−2−2cot2⁡2s=−2csc2⁡2s.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

If f(x,y)=ex+2y,x=s2, and y=s, compute dfds.

a
s2es2+2s
b
2(s+2)es2+2s
c
s(s+2)es2+2s
d
2ses2+2s
e
2(s+1)es2+2s

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(s)=e^(s²+2s). The chain rule gives df/ds=(2s+2)e^(s²+2s)=2(s+1)e^(s²+2s), matching option e.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+2y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 2s+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 1 \\  & =2s{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s} \\  & =2(s+1){e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

If f(x,y)=ex+2y,x=s2, and y=s, compute dfds.

a
s2es2+2s
b
2(s+2)es2+2s
c
s(s+2)es2+2s
d
2ses2+2s
e
2(s+1)es2+2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ex+2y,∂f∂y=2ex+2y

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=es2+2s,∂f∂y=2es2+2s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=2s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=es2+2s⋅2s+2es2+2s⋅1=2ses2+2s+2es2+2s=2(s+1)es2+2s.

∂f∂x=ex+2y,∂f∂y=2ex+2y

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=es2+2s,∂f∂y=2es2+2s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=2s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=es2+2s⋅2s+2es2+2s⋅1=2ses2+2s+2es2+2s=2(s+1)es2+2s.

If f(x,y)=cos⁡(x2+y) and y=1x, compute dfdx.

a
(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x)
b
(1+4x2)cos⁡(x2−1x)
c
(1−4x3x)cos⁡(x3+1x2)
d
(2x2+1x)sin⁡(x3+1x)
e
(1−3x3)sin⁡(x2+1x2)
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=1/x gives f(x)=cos(x²+1/x). Thus df/dx=−sin(x²+1/x)(2x−1/x²)=[(1−2x³)/x²]sin((x³+1)/x), matching option a.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}

Question 6
?

If f(x,y)=cos⁡(x2+y) and y=1x, compute dfdx.

a
(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x)
b
(1+4x2)cos⁡(x2−1x)
c
(1−4x3x)cos⁡(x3+1x2)
d
(2x2+1x)sin⁡(x3+1x)
e
(1−3x3)sin⁡(x2+1x2)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+y),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+y)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+1x).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=−1x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x)+(−sin⁡(x2+1x))⋅(−1x2)=(1x2−2x)sin⁡(x2+1x)=(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x).

verification.explanation: Differentiating cos(x²+1/x) gives −sin(x²+1/x)(2x−1/x²)=[(1−2x³)/x²]sin((x³+1)/x). This confirms option a and agrees with the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case

history.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+y),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+y)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+1x).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=−1x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x)+(−sin⁡(x2+1x))⋅(−1x2)=(1x2−2x)sin⁡(x2+1x)=(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x).

Your Answer:
(1−4x3x)cos⁡(x3+1x2)

Question 7
?

If f(x,y)=1x+y and y=e−x, compute dfdx.

a
 1−2e−x(x+e−x)2
b
 e−x1+xe−x
c
 1−e−x1+xe−x
d
 2(x+e−x)2
e
−1+e−x(x+e−x)2
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(x)=(x+e^(−x))^(−1). The chain rule gives df/dx=−(1−e^(−x))/(x+e^(−x))², matching option e.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}\cdot (-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1+{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

If f(x,y)=1x+y and y=e−x, compute dfdx.

a
 1−2e−x(x+e−x)2
b
 e−x1+xe−x
c
 1−e−x1+xe−x
d
 2(x+e−x)2
e
−1+e−x(x+e−x)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=−1(x+y)2,∂f∂y=−1(x+y)2

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=∂f∂y=−1(x+e−x)2.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=−e−x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=−1(x+e−x)2−1(x+e−x)2⋅(−e−x)=−1(x+e−x)2+e−x(x+e−x)2=−1+e−x(x+e−x)2.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}\cdot (-{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}+\frac{{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1+{e}^{-x}}{(x+{e}^{-x})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(x)=x³/(x+1). The quotient rule gives df/dx=[3x²(x+1)−x³]/(x+1)²=x²(2x+3)/(x+1)², matching option b.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

b

c

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y(x+1)2,∂f∂y=1x+1

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−x3(x+1)2,∂f∂y=1x+1.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=3x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−x3(x+1)2+1x+1⋅3x2=3x2x+1−x3(x+1)2=3x2(x+1)−x3(x+1)2=3x3+3x2−x3(x+1)2=x2(2x+3)(x+1)2.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

If f(x,y)=x2+yx and y=sin⁡x, compute dfdx.

a
 2x+xsin⁡x
b
 2x+sin⁡x+cos⁡xsin⁡x
c
2x+sin⁡x+xcos⁡x
d
 2x+sin⁡x+cos⁡x
e
 2x+sin⁡x−2sin⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2x+y,∂f∂y=x

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=2x+sin⁡x∂f∂y=x.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=cos⁡x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=2x+sin⁡x+xcos⁡x.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

If f(x,y)=yln⁡(x2+1) and y=x2+1, compute dfdx.

a
2xln⁡(x2+1)
b
2x(x2+1)ln⁡(x2+1)
c
2xln⁡(x2+1)
d
(x2+1)ln⁡(x2+1)
e
2x(1+ln⁡(x2+1))

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(x)=(x²+1)ln(x²+1). The product rule gives df/dx=2x ln(x²+1)+2x=2x(1+ln(x²+1)), matching option e.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

If f(x,y)=yln⁡(x2+1) and y=x2+1, compute dfdx.

a
2xln⁡(x2+1)
b
2x(x2+1)ln⁡(x2+1)
c
2xln⁡(x2+1)
d
(x2+1)ln⁡(x2+1)
e
2x(1+ln⁡(x2+1))
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xyx2+1,∂f∂y=ln⁡(x2+1)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=2x(x2+1)x2+1=2x,∂f∂y=ln⁡(x2+1).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=2x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=2x+ln⁡(x2+1)⋅2x=2x(1+ln⁡(x2+1)).

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(st))(s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st))+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(st))(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st)) \\  & =s{cos}^{2}⁡(st)-s{sin}^{2}⁡(st) \\  & =s({cos}^{2}⁡(st)-{sin}^{2}⁡(st)) \\  & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(2st).\end{aligned}
$$

a

b

c

e

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=y,∂f∂y=x

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=cos⁡(st),∂f∂y=sin⁡(st).

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=scos⁡(st),∂y∂t=−ssin⁡(st).

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=(cos⁡(st))(scos⁡(st))+(sin⁡(st))(−ssin⁡(st))=scos2⁡(st)−ssin2⁡(st)=s(cos2⁡(st)−sin2⁡(st))=scos⁡(2st).

Let f(x,y)=yex, where x=t+s and y=ts. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
tet+s(s−t)
b
set+s(t+1)
c
set+s
d
tet+s(s+1)
e
et+s(s+t)
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(s,t)=ts e^(t+s). Holding t constant, the product rule gives ∂f/∂s=t e^(t+s)+ts e^(t+s)=t e^(t+s)(s+1), matching option d.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(ts{e}^{t+s})(1)+({e}^{t+s})(t) \\  & =t{e}^{t+s}(s+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12

Let f(x,y)=yex, where x=t+s and y=ts. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
tet+s(s−t)
b
set+s(t+1)
c
set+s
d
tet+s(s+1)
e
et+s(s+t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows:

∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=yex,∂f∂y=ex

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get

∂f∂x=tset+s,∂f∂y=et+s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

∂x∂s=1,∂y∂s=t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(tset+s)(1)+(et+s)(t)=tet+s(s+1).

verification.explanation: Holding t constant, differentiating ts e^(t+s) with respect to s gives t e^(t+s)+ts e^(t+s)=t e^(t+s)(s+1). This confirms option d and agrees with the revealed solution.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2+t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =s{e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2+t{e}^{s})(0)+(s{e}^{s})({e}^{s}) \\  & =s{e}^{2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Let f(x,y)=xy2−2y, where x=st2 and y=s3−t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
3s6t2−6s2+t4
b
7s6t2−8s3t3−6s2+t4
c
4s3t3−5s2+2t4
d
7s3t2−4s3t3−6s
e
7s5t2+2s3t3−6s2+4t2
Submit

decision.explanation: Holding t constant, the chain rule gives ∂f/∂s=t²(s³−t)²+[2st²(s³−t)−2](3s²). Expanding yields 7s⁶t²−8s³t³−6s²+t⁴, matching option b.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy-2\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =({s}^{3}-t)^{2}={s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(s{t}^{2})({s}^{3}-t)-2=2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =({s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2})({t}^{2})+(2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2)(3{s}^{2}) \\  & ={s}^{6}{t}^{2}-2{s}^{3}{t}^{3}+{t}^{4}+6{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-6{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2} \\  & =7{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-8{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2}+{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Let f(x,y)=xy2−2y, where x=st2 and y=s3−t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
3s6t2−6s2+t4
b
7s6t2−8s3t3−6s2+t4
c
4s3t3−5s2+2t4
d
7s3t2−4s3t3−6s
e
7s5t2+2s3t3−6s2+4t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=y2,∂f∂y=2xy−2

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=(s3−t)2=s6−2s3t+t2,∂f∂y=2(st2)(s3−t)−2=2s4t2−2st3−2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=t2,∂y∂s=3s2.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(s6−2s3t+t2)(t2)+(2s4t2−2st3−2)(3s2)=s6t2−2s3t3+t4+6s6t2−6s3t3−6s2=7s6t2−8s3t3−6s2+t4.

verification.explanation: Substituting and expanding gives f(s,t)=s⁷t²−2s⁴t³+st⁴−2s³+2t. Holding t constant, ∂f/∂s=7s⁶t²−8s³t³−6s²+t⁴. This confirms option b and agrees with the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy-2\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =({s}^{3}-t)^{2}={s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(s{t}^{2})({s}^{3}-t)-2=2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =({s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2})({t}^{2})+(2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2)(3{s}^{2}) \\  & ={s}^{6}{t}^{2}-2{s}^{3}{t}^{3}+{t}^{4}+6{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-6{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2} \\  & =7{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-8{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2}+{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Let f(x,y)=xy, where x=cos⁡t+sin⁡s and y=sin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+sin⁡scos⁡t
b
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+cos⁡ssin⁡t
c
cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t+cos⁡scos⁡t
d
1+cos⁡scos⁡t
e
1+sin⁡ssin⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=y,∂f∂y=x

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=sin⁡t,∂f∂y=cos⁡t+sin⁡s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=−sin⁡t,∂y∂t=cos⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=sin⁡t(−sin⁡t)+(cos⁡t+sin⁡s)⋅cos⁡t=−sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t+sin⁡scos⁡t.

\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y+z}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{s+t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{s+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}\cdot (1)+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{-({s}^{2}+{t}^{2})+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2ts-{s}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=-1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=1,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=-1+2+1=2.
$$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y+z}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{s+t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{s+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}\cdot (1)+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{-({s}^{2}+{t}^{2})+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2ts-{s}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=-1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=1,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=-1+2+1=2.
$$

Question 17
?

Let f(x,y,z)=x2y−5yz, where x=st, y=s3 and z=ssin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
5s4t−5s3sin⁡t
b
3s4t2+10s3sin⁡t
c
2s2t4−20ssin⁡t
d
5s4t2−20s3sin⁡t
e
5s2t4−15ssin⁡t−5sin⁡t
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(s,t)=s⁵t²−5s⁴sin(t). Holding t constant, ∂f/∂s=5s⁴t²−20s³sin(t), matching option d.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 17
?

Let f(x,y,z)=x2y−5yz, where x=st, y=s3 and z=ssin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
5s4t−5s3sin⁡t
b
3s4t2+10s3sin⁡t
c
2s2t4−20ssin⁡t
d
5s4t2−20s3sin⁡t
e
5s2t4−15ssin⁡t−5sin⁡t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=2xy,∂f∂y=x2−5z,∂f∂z=−5y.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=2(st)(s3)=2s4t,∂f∂y=(st)2−5(ssin⁡t)=s2t2−5ssin⁡t,∂f∂z=−5s3.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=t,∂y∂s=3s2,∂z∂s=sin⁡t.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=(2s4t)⋅t+(s2t2−5ssin⁡t)⋅3s2+(−5s3)⋅sin⁡t=2s4t2+3s4t2−15s3sin⁡t−5s3sin⁡t=5s4t2−20s3sin⁡t.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+{s}^{2})}=-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2ts, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}})\cdot 2ts+(-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}))\cdot (\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}})+(4)\cdot 2s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-4s+8s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}+4s \\  & =\frac{2(1+2{s}^{2})}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=1x,∂f∂y=−2ey,∂f∂z=4.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=1ts2,∂f∂y=−2eln⁡(t2+s2)=−2(t2+s2),∂f∂z=4.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=2ts,∂y∂s=2st2+s2,∂z∂s=2s.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=(1ts2)⋅2ts+(−2(t2+s2))⋅(2st2+s2)+(4)⋅2s=2s−4s+8s=2s+4s=2(1+2s2)s.

verification.explanation: Holding t constant, the chain rule gives ∂f/∂s=(1/(ts²))(2ts)−2(t²+s²)(2s/(t²+s²))+4(2s)=2/s+4s=2(1+2s²)/s. This confirms option c and agrees with the revealed solution.

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+{s}^{2})}=-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =4.\end{aligned}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2ts, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =2s.\end{aligned}

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}})\cdot 2ts+(-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}))\cdot (\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}})+(4)\cdot 2s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-4s+8s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}+4s \\  & =\frac{2(1+2{s}^{2})}{s}.\end{aligned}

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(t+2s)=2t+4s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(3t-s)=6t-2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2t+4s)\cdot 2+(6t-2s)\cdot (-1)+(2st)\cdot t \\  & =4t+8s-6t+2s+2s{t}^{2} \\  & =10s-2t+2s{t}^{2} \\  & =2(5s-t+s{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(t+2s)=2t+4s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(3t-s)=6t-2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2t+4s)\cdot 2+(6t-2s)\cdot (-1)+(2st)\cdot t \\  & =4t+8s-6t+2s+2s{t}^{2} \\  & =10s-2t+2s{t}^{2} \\  & =2(5s-t+s{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Let f(x,y,z)=xyz, where x=2, y=set and z=tes. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
2t(s+1)et+s
b
2s(t+1)et+s
c
4t(s−1)et+s
d
4(t−s)et+s
e
2(t+s)et+s
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting gives f(s,t)=2st e^(t+s). Holding s constant, ∂f/∂t=2s e^(t+s)+2st e^(t+s)=2s(t+1)e^(t+s), matching option b.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=xz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2s{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =s{e}^{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(ts{e}^{t+s})\cdot 0+(2t{e}^{s})\cdot s{e}^{t}+(2s{e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{s} \\  & =2ts{e}^{t+s}+2s{e}^{t+s} \\  & =2s(t+1){e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

Let f(x,y,z)=xyz, where x=2, y=set and z=tes. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
2t(s+1)et+s
b
2s(t+1)et+s
c
4t(s−1)et+s
d
4(t−s)et+s
e
2(t+s)et+s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=yz,∂f∂y=xz,∂f∂z=xy.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=tset+s,∂f∂y=2tes,∂f∂z=2set.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=0,∂y∂t=set,∂z∂t=es.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂t=(tset+s)⋅0+(2tes)⋅set+(2set)⋅es=2tset+s+2set+s=2s(t+1)et+s.

content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044606/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=xz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2s{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =s{e}^{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(ts{e}^{t+s})\cdot 0+(2t{e}^{s})\cdot s{e}^{t}+(2s{e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{s} \\  & =2ts{e}^{t+s}+2s{e}^{t+s} \\  & =2s(t+1){e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$
